ch01.summary: The reader can now write a recursive backtracking matcher for literal, dot, concatenation and star, trace by hand which alternatives a star tries and in what order, and predict whether a failing case grows linearly, polynomially or exponentially. code/backtrack.py exists with match_here (does the pattern match at the start of the text), match_star (longest run first, then give back one character at a time) and search (every start position). Listing 1-1 is code/blowup.py, Python's re on (a+)+b doubling per character; Listing 1-2 is backtrack.py; Listing 1-3 demos; Listing 1-4 times a*a*a*b at n=40..320 (about 8x per doubling, cubic); Listing 1-5 is the RecursionError on a 1,500-character pattern. Figure 1-1 is the give-back tree for a*a*b on aaa. The Stack Overflow 2016 and Cloudflare 2019 incidents are both presented as polynomial. Star height above one is stated as inexpressible in this language. Promised for chapter 2: a machine that can hold every abandoned path, plus +, ?, alternation and groups.

numbers.machine: Apple Silicon Mac, CPython 3.14, single run

ch02.summary: The reader can now parse the eight-construct language (literal, dot, concatenation, star, plus, optional, alternation, group) into an abstract syntax tree, compile the tree into a graph of states by Thompson's construction, walk and count the states of any pattern, and explain why a pattern of m non-parenthesis characters compiles to exactly m+1 states. code/nodes.py defines Char, Dot, Concat, Alt and Repeat (Repeat carries min and many instead of three classes). code/parse.py is a recursive-descent Parser with one method per precedence level (alt, concat, repeat, atom) and a parse() entry; it rejects a second quantifier with 'multiple repeat' and an unclosed group with 'missing )'. code/machine.py defines State (ch, out, alt, matched; eq=False), compile_node(node, cont) in the book's own 'continuation style' (two-endpoint idea credited to Jules Jacobs), and compile_pattern. Listing 2-6 walks (a|b)*c into six states; Listing 2-7 shows states = chars + 1 on six patterns. Figure 2-1 is the two kinds of state; Figure 2-2 is the five fragments. The aside quotes Thompson's a** remark and notes (a*)* still parses and compiles to a cycle of splits. Promised for chapter 3: run the machine holding every live state at once, bounded by m+1 states per step, and survive the split cycle using the dedup idea from Thompson's closing notes.

figures.2-2: fragments for ab, a|b, a*, a+, a?

ch03.summary: The reader can now run chapter 2's machine over a text as a set of live states, one step per character, explain why the work per character is bounded by the pattern (at most m+1 states, so O(n*m) overall), and name the one check that both bounds the live set and terminates a cycle of splits. code/simulate.py defines add_state (follows splits eagerly, dedups by id(s) in seen), step (live set before a character to live set after it), fullmatch and an unanchored search that re-enters the start state before every character. code/tinyre.py is the public API: compile, fullmatch, search and class Pattern with fullmatch and search methods. Listing 3-5 is code/bench.py, backtrack vs tinyre vs re on a*a*a*b; Listing 3-6 measures a*b at n=800,000 where re is about 450x faster; Listing 3-7 removes seen and shows the RecursionError on (a*)*b. Figure 3-1 is the live-set timeline of (a|b)*c over abc. The set records which states are live, not how: captures need the Pike VM's threads, backreferences cannot be done this way (NP-complete per Cox). Promised for chapter 4: exhaustive comparison against re on every pattern up to four characters, the mismatch the first version had, and the full list of what tinyre gave up and what RE2, Go and Rust do instead.

ch04.summary: The reader can now enumerate every small pattern and short string, run tinyre against re on all of them, read a mismatch report and classify the fault as simulator, parser or meaning, list what tinyre gave up (anchors, classes, Unicode, captures, lazy and possessive quantifiers, lookaround, backreferences) with what RE2 and Python re do for each, and name the automata engines (RE2, Go regexp, Rust regex, .NET 7 NonBacktracking) against the backtracking defaults (Perl, PCRE, Python, Java, JavaScript), including the terminology trap that PCRE and Java call backtracking 'NFA'. code/difftest.py enumerates patterns of up to 4 pieces over nine pieces and strings of up to 3 letters over ab, skipping what either engine rejects, comparing fullmatch only. Listing 4-1 is difftest.py (10080 cases, 0 mismatches); Listing 4-2 prints 672 patterns, 15 strings, 10,080 cases, 0 mismatches; Listing 4-3 is the expect-error for tinyre.compile('a+?') ('multiple repeat at 2'); Listing 4-4 monkeypatches machine.compile_node so a? compiles as a and shows 334 mismatches with the five smallest cases printed. The story: the first parser allowed a second quantifier, so a+? parsed as (a+)? and a?+ as (a?)+; the test found 171 mismatches in 11,970 cases over 56 patterns, all stacked quantifiers, because Python reads +? as lazy and ?+ as possessive (3.11+); resolved by refusing with 'multiple repeat'. Figure 4-1 is Rust's engine ladder (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA, bounded backtracker, PikeVM). Closes with 'What this book did not cover': classes, anchors, Unicode, captures, POSIX vs Perl semantics, DFAs; next reads are Cox 2007 on caching the NFA into a DFA and Cox 2009 on the Pike VM. No forward tension; last chapter.
